If immigration judges can be fired for deciding independently, they aren't judges. Congress *could* create a genuinely independent Article I immigration court, but it has chosen not to. There are no immigration judges left: only deportation judges.

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

Remember that the administration fired immigration judges on day one. This ruling tells those judges they have no recourse and sends a message to every remaining judge that if your rulings don't fall in line, you're out. 

I've written about this before: austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

Most people don't know that immigration judges were never truly independent. They're DOJ employees, subject in many ways to the AG's direction. Civil service tenure was the last floor of protection against being fired for ruling the wrong way but the MSPB just removed that floor.

A federal board just ruled that immigration judges can be fired at will by the president, stripping the civil service protections meant to insulate them from political interference. This is a HUGE deal for asylum seekers and the courts.

Hays County, TX is finalizing a 287(g) agreement with ICE under SB 8, that requires sheriffs to partner with federal imm enforcement. Officials say they’ll adopt the least intrusive model, while local leaders raise concerns about past enforcement actions.

Trump’s Deportation Machine is Getting a Reality Check

The Supreme Court looks ready to reject Trump’s birthright citizenship order, DHS has paused its warehouse detention expansion, and even red-state sheriffs are saying no.

His attorney, Margaret Stock, is an amazing professional; she does a great job adding context. Great reporting below, read it to learn more about the long-standing practical challenges of proving citizenship. 

alaskapublic.org/news/anchor…

The latest case involves a 12-year-old Alaskan boy whom immigration officials are working to deport while his attorney tries to keep him in the U.S. by proving his father is a citizen. But the dad, a vet and gov employee, is avoiding a paternity test, and doing little to help.

The Supreme Court may well reject the Trump admin's wild thesis about birthright citizenship, but that doesn't mean that the complications of proving citizenship are fixed. The immigration system has long generated challenges/hurdles both intentionally and incidentally.

Pam Bondi is out. Trump just fired the AG who spent the last year politicizing the DOJ, failing to deliver the Epstein Files (as Congress req'd), and undermining the federal courts. She won't be missed, but unlikely that a replacement will be different.

The deaths that don't appear in official data may actually be more revealing of how this system works than the ones that do. The official count is not the full picture, it's the portion the system has so far failed to conceal.

A CNN review found that of ~72,000 people who self-deported through Project Homecoming, more than half were in ICE detention when they signed up. Suffering inside facilities functions as coercion, pressure to leave rather than fight.

cnn.com/2026/03/18/us/dhs-se…

This is what scholars call the "administrative production of death" not a bullet, but a sustained arrangement of institutions, contracts, and procedural choices that make death statistically predictable. I've written more on this here:

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

There's a concept from systems thinking called POSIWID: "the purpose of a system is what it does." The question isn't what ICE says detention is for, it's what it reliably produces. And what it produces is preventable death without accountability.

en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_pu…

I am not arguing that any administration has a policy of intentionally killing detained immigrants, at least not in the subjective sense. What the evidence supports is that the system is structured to make death predictable and structured to avoid accountability for it.

A March 2026 KFF analysis found that 32 of 46 ICE deaths between Jan. 2025 and March 2026 involved people with pre-existing conditions whose health worsened in custody. ICE blames the conditions. But people are dying of preventable things.

kff.org/racial-equity-and-he…

EX: the Deadly Failures report discussed Johana Medina Leon, a 25-yr-old asylum seeker, was found unconscious in her cell. Hours later, ICE served her release paperwork at her bedside, listed as "released" in critical condition. She died 4 days later, not in official death stats.
In some documented cases, ICE has officially "released" critically ill detainees while they are still hospitalized, a bookkeeping maneuver to avoid counting their deaths in official reports.

Category 3: Post-release deaths and "pre-death releases." Once someone leaves ICE custody, they fall off the system's ledger entirely. ICE has a directive allowing review of deaths within 30 days of release but has apparently never used it.

The prevalence and fear of death gives the impression that simply getting out of detention alive is enough. ICE, like Billy Crystal's Miracle Max in Princess Bride, produces the situation for people to be "not completely dead, only mostly dead" by the time they get out.
